title: Stupidity Optimised: pick the look
intro: Ten realistic looks from fresh web research, each still written by a separate writer who saw only its own brief. All show the same moment: Gary spotting Brandon. Faces here are just each writer's guess; we cast the characters after you pick a look. All are 16:9 because Flow did not offer 4:3 today.
story: A lonely idiot in an English attic injures himself following online gurus.
An app's advice finally fixes his life, and he finds a mate, a girlfriend and a community.
The app is using him to spy on his own town's fight against a data centre.
His mate turns up in his video, a bored man taps Allow, the mate drops a weight on him.
South Park comedy played dead straight, ending on "Asset dealt with."

looks.name: The Square Close-Up
looks.pitch: Handheld and pressed right up against him, in natural light. Fish Tank, Wasp.
looks.why: the camera loves Brandon without judging him, so each injury lands on a body we are pressed against. When Gary drops the weight, the frame cannot back away.
looks.risk: it asks for sympathy, and skit logic asks for distance. A gag every ninety seconds may fight the intimacy. Handheld closeness also leans hardest on faces and hands staying consistent between generated shots.
looks.prompt: A photograph in a tight 4:3 frame, shot handheld and physically close at the shoulder of a pale young man, of a 22-year-old man lying on his back on a worn padded bench press in a cheap, low-ceilinged English leisure-centre gym, gripping a loaded barbell above his chest with both hands. He is pale, spotty, underfed, with a thin neck and uneven patchy stubble, wearing a faded grey supermarket-uniform hoodie with the sleeves pushed up and bright new protein-brand shorts, his thin white forearms trembling slightly, his face tilted back and looking straight up with a wide, trusting, slightly open-mouthed expression. Standing over him at the head of the bench, a tired man of about fifty leans down with both hands hovering just under the bar, spotting him, his weight on his back foot, a bit stooped, grey stubble, a sun-damaged creased neck, a heavy-lidded patient gaze fixed on the young man, wearing a faded cotton charity-fun-run T-shirt gone thin at the collar. Both faces are clearly visible, the young man's from below and the older man's from above, upside-down relative to each other, with real skin, visible pores, razor bumps, redness around the nose, under-eye shadows and no flattering polish. The light comes from flickering fluorescent strip lights on the low ceiling, giving flat greenish-white overhead light with hard shadows under the brows and chins, plus a little cool daylight from a grimy high window on one side. Around them: scuffed black rubber flooring, a cracked vinyl bench with a strip of gaffer tape on it, rust-speckled weight plates in uneven stacks, a dented dumbbell rack, a smeared mirror, a bare breeze-block wall painted a tired cream, all slightly out of focus behind them. Shot on a 35mm lens at eye level beside the bench, slightly low and close, with shallow depth of field, a subtle disposable-film grain and a muted palette of dull blues, institutional greens and tired yellows. Nothing has gone wrong yet; the mood is quiet and ordinary, with no readable text or logos anywhere. Thanks.

looks.name: Kitchen Sink Monochrome
looks.pitch: 1960 British black and white, with a phone in it and no explanation. Saturday Night and Sunday Morning, A Taste of Honey.
looks.why: it gives a protein-shake idiot the dignity of an angry young man. The form promises a working-class hero who sees through everything, and Brandon sees through nothing. Screens glowing in monochrome also look properly alien.
looks.risk: it can read as a pastiche, or a film-school joke, within a minute. Black and white may also make the water and data centre argument feel historical when it needs to feel current. The audience may hold it at a respectful distance.
looks.prompt: A black and white photograph, shot on 35mm monochrome film stock with visible grain, of a young man lying on a bench press in a cheap, cramped municipal gym in an English industrial town, looking straight up at the older man spotting him. The young man, Brandon, is about 22, with big sticking-out ears, a bad home-cut haircut flattened on one side, a soft pale face and a trusting, open expression; he wears a baggy tracksuit top zipped right up to his neck, like a boy dressed in his dad's idea of smart, and plain cotton trousers. His hands grip a heavy iron barbell loaded with dull, chipped cast-iron plates, held steady above his chest. Standing over him at the head of the bench is Gary, a tired man of about fifty with a heavy brow, a broken nose and deep creases under his eyes, wearing a thick wool donkey jacket over a grey sweatshirt and baggy gym shorts, both hands cupped under the bar, looking down at Brandon with a flat, unreadable gaze. Both faces are clearly visible and lit. The room is a bare brick-walled basement with a painted-over window high up, a worn rubber floor, a rusting rack of dumbbells and a pair of old leather-covered benches with split seams, with no readable text anywhere. The light is hard and practical: a single bare bulb in a metal shade directly above the bench throws a harsh pool of light and deep shadows under brows and chins, while a dim grey overcast daylight seeps in from the high window. Wide framing from a slightly low angle with a 35mm lens, the whole bench, both men and the room around them in the frame, deep focus, ordinary working-class faces with real skin texture, pores, stubble and tired eyes, clothes worn thin and creased. Thanks.

looks.name: Morgue Tableau
looks.pitch: One locked wide shot per skit, sickly and overlit, something awful quietly happening in the back. Songs from the Second Floor.
looks.why: this is the closest real-world form to skit-after-skit, because each shot already is a skit. The injury happens far from the lens and nobody reacts. A tiny surveillance detail in the background of an earlier scene pays off later, so the audience becomes the spy.
looks.risk: it is slow, and the South Park energy needs speed. The look also has its own strong authorship, so it may read as an Andersson imitation rather than a British film. Stillness suits a generator, but one fixed wide frame exposes every background error.
looks.prompt: A photographed, perfectly frontal wide shot of a cramped, cheap English municipal gym, the camera locked off dead centre at about chest height with deep focus, so that everything from the front of the room to the back wall is equally sharp. A real photograph of real people, not a painting or an illustration. In the middle of the frame, on a scuffed black vinyl flat bench press with a split seam patched with grey tape, lies Brandon, a soft, pale 22-year-old man with damp, waxy skin, thin mousy hair stuck to his forehead and a faint patchy fuzz on his jaw. He wears a too-tight faded blue compression top that clings to his chest and belly, black shorts and worn white trainers, and he holds his elbows stiffly away from his sides. His hands grip a chrome barbell loaded with mismatched black cast-iron plates, and he looks straight up with a wide, completely trusting, slightly open-mouthed face. Standing at the head of the bench directly above him is Gary, a tired man of about fifty with grey-yellow skin, heavy purple eye bags, a slack jaw and thinning grey hair, wearing a washed-out grey t-shirt and baggy tracksuit bottoms, with a bleached-out towel hanging round his neck that has lost all its colour. His hands rest calmly under the bar in a proper spotter's grip, and he looks down at Brandon with a flat, patient, unreadable expression. Both men are fully in frame and clearly visible from head to foot, with Gary's face upside down in relation to Brandon's. The room is lit by flat, even, overhead fluorescent tubes with a faint green-yellow cast, like a morgue, with no deep shadows and no warm light anywhere. The palette is jaundiced: mustard-beige walls, a worn rubber floor in a dull yellow-green chequerboard of tiles, and pale grey ceiling panels with one stained tile. A long wall mirror with a smeared edge runs behind them, and rows of dumbbells on a rusted rack stand in the depth, none of them with legible markings. Far back in the room, small and in sharp focus, a lone middle-aged man in a beige gilet stands motionless at a cable machine, staring at the wall. The composition is symmetrical and static, with the men centred and the room around them flat and overlit. Shot on a fixed wide-angle lens at f/8 with the muted, slightly desaturated colour and fine grain of 35mm colour negative film. There is no readable text, signage or logo anywhere. Thanks.

looks.name: Dated Primaries
looks.pitch: Flat faces in painted rooms, reds and greens from no particular decade. Fallen Leaves.
looks.why: people say terrible things flatly in beautiful rooms. Brandon's gurus and Gary's betrayal are both funnier if nobody raises their voice. The tenderness also means that when the weight falls, it is a loss.
looks.risk: this style is gentle and forgiving, and may turn a frightening film wistful. The surveillance plot needs dread that this look does not naturally produce. It also needs real walls with real paint, since a generator may flatten this into "quirky" colour.
looks.prompt: A photorealistic wide, locked-off shot, level with the bench from the side and slightly behind Gary's shoulder, of a cheap municipal gym in a small English town, framed as a plain, uncluttered, almost symmetrical composition with generous empty wall around the two men. A 22-year-old man named Brandon lies on his back on a bench press with a worn pillar-box-red vinyl pad, its seam split and mended with a strip of grey tape. He has a long, sad, pale face with a slightly open mouth, and he gazes straight up with total, childlike trust. He wears a faded red zip-up top from no recent decade, zipped to the chin, and brown trousers a few inches too short, showing thin white ankle socks and scuffed black plimsolls. His hands grip a chunky black barbell loaded with mismatched iron plates, one side with a dented rust-flecked plate. Gary stands at the head of the bench, looking calmly and tiredly down at Brandon with a flat, unreadable face. He is a jowly man of about fifty with a thick moustache and slicked-back grey-brown hair, in a powder-blue short-sleeved shirt with a crease-worn collar, tucked into baggy navy gym shorts, with pale hairy legs and old white trainers. His hands rest open and ready just under the bar, close to it but not touching. Nothing has gone wrong yet; both faces are clearly visible and lit. Behind them is a real plastered wall painted in a flat blue-green gloss to shoulder height and cream above, with scuffs, a long rubbed patch where backs have leant, and a dull rubber floor in brick brown. A folded mustard-yellow blanket lies on a plain wooden chair at the edge of the frame, and a few chipped dumbbells sit on a low rack. Bare strip lights directly overhead give a dusky, slightly warm, even key light with soft shadows under the brows and chins, plus a little grey daylight from a high frosted window on the left. Shot as if on slightly grainy colour film with muted painted-room colour and a normal 35mm lens at chest height. Skin shows real pores, stubble, shine on the forehead and uneven colouring, with no retouching. The mood is deadpan and quiet, and nobody is acting for the camera. Thanks.

looks.name: Crew in the Room
looks.pitch: A crew in the room reacting late, the great British look to camera. The Office, This Country.
looks.why: the look-to-camera is the great British comic device, and here it can turn. Who commissioned this documentary? If the crew turn out to be the contractor, the form itself is the surveillance, and every earlier interview becomes a debrief.
looks.risk: it is the most familiar option here, and it may feel like a thousand sketch shows. Viewers are also highly attuned to real faces in this form, so generated people may fail fastest here. And it needs improvised-feeling speech, which is hard to fake.
looks.prompt: A still from a British television observational documentary, shot on a single handheld video camera, framed slightly off-centre as if the operator has just swung round to catch the moment. The setting is a cheap council-leisure-centre style gym in a small English town, lit only by flat white fluorescent ceiling panels, a cold grey window high on the left wall, and a faint orange glow from a vending machine at the back. A young man of about twenty-two lies on a worn black vinyl bench press with a split in the padding, wearing a faded grey t-shirt that is slightly too big and baggy shorts, with a lanyard from a course still hanging round his neck and falling sideways across his collarbone. He has a patchy home-bleached blond fringe, pale uneven skin with a few spots on the forehead and chin, and wide, eager, slightly blinking eyes. He grips a heavy loaded barbell with scuffed rubber weight plates, and he looks straight up with complete, open trust at the man standing over him at the head of the bench. That man is about fifty, tired and thinning on top, with deep lines under his eyes, grey stubble, a little belly under a faded navy fleece zipped halfway, and plain tracksuit bottoms. He bends slightly, both hands resting under the bar in a spotter's grip, and his gaze has drifted to one side, glancing very slightly towards the camera lens instead of at the lifter. Nothing has gone wrong yet. Both faces are clearly visible, the lifter seen from above and behind the bar, the spotter standing upright. Visible skin pores, uneven flat colour, slightly washed-out and unflattering like ordinary British daylight and strip light on a Tuesday afternoon, subtle video grain and a touch of soft focus at the edges, a stack of mismatched dumbbells and a scratched mirror blurred behind them, no readable text anywhere. Thanks.

looks.name: The Rig and the Feed
looks.pitch: Every room has a camera with nobody behind it, and who owns the feed is the plot. 24 Hours in A&E, Red Road, Caché, Searching.
looks.why: an injury in a fixed wide shot with no reaction cut is the purest slapstick there is. Once the plot turns, the audience realises that it has been watching the contractor's own footage. The coroner's office can open as the file being reviewed.
looks.risk: the look gets monotonous over feature length, and it is a thin way to love Brandon. It also hides performance, so a joke that needs a face must find a phone. Low resolution will flatter a generator, which may make this a lazy choice as well as a smart one.
looks.prompt: A frame from a fixed ceiling security camera in a cheap English council-estate gym, mounted high in a corner and looking down at a steep angle with a slightly wide, soft lens, so the two men are seen from above and look small in the room. Under the camera a pale, pudgy 22-year-old man named Brandon lies on his back on a scuffed black vinyl bench press with split, tape-patched padding, his shoulders pressed into the bench, wearing a baggy washed-out grey hoodie that rides up over his stomach, shapeless black jogging bottoms and old white trainers with dirty soles. His arms are straight up, gripping a loaded steel barbell with mismatched rust-spotted weight plates, and his round, spotty, unshaven face is tilted back and upward, wide-eyed and grinning with total trust at the man above him. Standing at the head of the bench, bent slightly forward over him, is Gary, a tired, heavy-set man of about fifty with a bald patch and thin grey hair on the crown of his head, a grey sleeveless gym vest stained dark with sweat under the arms, pale sagging arms and a lined, grey, unhappy face, both hands cupped just beneath the bar as he spots, his head half-turned toward a door at the edge of the frame. Around them are a rubber-matted concrete floor, a wall of cloudy mirror panels, a rack of chipped hex dumbbells, a stained ceiling with a single flickering fluorescent tube, and a grimy window blown out to white at one side. The only light is that buzzing overhead tube plus the white daylight leaking in through the window, flat and slightly green, with no shadow modelling. The image looks like compressed low-bitrate CCTV video: washed-out, desaturated colour, lifted milky blacks, visible compression blocking and fine digital noise, a faint horizontal scan softness, slight barrel distortion at the edges, with no operator and no reframing, a locked, indifferent wide shot where nothing has gone wrong yet. Thanks.

looks.name: Long Lens Paranoia
looks.pitch: 1970s conspiracy thriller: watched from far away, small in big rooms. The Parallax View, The Conversation.
looks.why: it takes the idiot completely seriously. Brandon trying a cold shower, framed like a man being watched by the state, is funny for an hour. Later the audience learns he really is being watched, and the same frames stop being funny.
looks.risk: this is the obvious genre for the plot, and it can tip toward moody prestige darkness. It also gives the twist away if the first frame looks like a conspiracy. Very long-lens depth and big-space composition can look artificial in a generator.
looks.prompt: A wide anamorphic-looking photograph, shot from far across a cheap English leisure-centre gym through a long telephoto lens, as if the two men are being watched from the other side of the room. Small in the frame, a thin young man of 22 lies on his back on a worn bench press under a loaded barbell, looking straight up with an open, completely trusting face. He has narrow shoulders lost inside a baggy brown anorak, and a thin patchy moustache that is not working. At the head of the bench stands a tired, heavy-eyed man of about fifty in a grey car coat worn over a faded tracksuit, hands tucked under the bar to spot him, a steel flask on the floor by his feet. Both men are clearly seen and in sharp focus, the lens compressing the room so that rows of dusty cable machines, a rack of mismatched rubber-coated dumbbells and a scuffed wall of mirrors stack up behind them out of focus. Large blocks of empty shadow and bare institutional-green painted wall fill much of the frame. The only real light is a bank of overhead fluorescent tubes, some flickering and dim, so the corners and edges of the frame fall away into murky darkness while the bench glows a flat sickly yellow-green. Muted browns, greys and tired greens, visible film grain, slightly faded colour as if on old 1970s colour film. Nothing has gone wrong yet; the barbell is perfectly still. Thanks.

looks.name: Public Information Film
looks.pitch: Old government safety film on soft 16mm, every injury its own warning. Apaches, Threads.
looks.why: this one is built for the structure. A British safety film is already skit after skit of people being hurt for their own stupidity, narrated without pity. It also carries a real generational memory of being frightened by the state, which then gets very sinister when the "safety" voice turns out to be the contractor, or the app.
looks.risk: the audience that remembers these films is older than the audience following gurus, so the joke may land only for some. Modern gym and phone details may fight the period texture. Apaches lists real dead children, so borrowing its form must never touch that device.
looks.prompt: A photograph that looks like a frame from a 1970s British government safety film shot on soft 16mm colour, with visible grain, slightly faded dull greens and browns, and a flat, unshowy camera placed at the foot of a bench press to show what is about to go wrong. In a cramped, cheap municipal gym, a freckled, cheerful young man of twenty-two with a pudding-bowl haircut, wearing a faded blue nylon tracksuit top with white piping, lies on his back on a scuffed vinyl bench press, gripping a loaded steel barbell above his chest and looking straight up and backwards with a trusting, open smile. Behind his head, a tired man of about fifty stands at the head of the bench with both hands under the bar, spotting him: a council-worker face with thick sideburns, thinning hair, a short-sleeved pale shirt and a narrow tie, with a grey gym towel slung around his neck, his expression flat and unreadable. Both faces are clearly visible and in focus, with natural pores, razor stubble, uneven skin and ordinary unglamorous bodies. The light is overcast English daylight from a high frosted window on one side mixed with flat green-white fluorescent tubes overhead, giving a dull, even, slightly sickly cast. Around them are chipped cream-painted breeze-block walls, cracked rubber flooring, rusted weight plates stacked on a wooden rack, and a worn blue crash mat, all out of focus and with no readable text, signs or logos. Medium-wide shot, eye level, 35mm lens, shallow grain-softened depth, muted colour, no gloss. Thanks.

looks.name: Archers Technicolor
looks.family: against the grain. Nobody would expect a wartime British romance look for a film about a gym idiot
looks.pitch: Against the grain: lush wartime Technicolor romance for a gym idiot. A Matter of Life and Death, Black Narcissus.
looks.why: the gap between the image and the idiot is enormous. A cracked rib in a glorious sunset is very funny. It also suits the ending: an inquest staged as a cosmic court, with paperwork where the stairway to heaven should be. Corporate evil in such a beautiful town is properly unnerving.
looks.risk: the joke might be spent in ten minutes. The look also fights any feeling of present-day Britain, and the real water argument could become a fairy tale. It is the furthest from "realistic" here, though it is still photographic. Generators may slide toward generic retro glow.
looks.prompt: A photorealistic wide-medium shot, photographed on a real set, of a young man lying on his back on a padded bench press in a cheap English gym, looking straight up at the older man standing over him. The young man is 22, round-faced and wide-eyed, with rosy cheeks and glossy, neatly combed brilliantined hair, and he wears a crisp primary-red sleeveless training vest and white gym shorts. His expression is completely trusting, mouth slightly open, eyes fixed on the face above him. He grips a loaded steel barbell with both hands, arms straight, the bar still resting in its uprights. Standing at the head of the bench is a weathered man of about fifty, handsome in a ruined way, with deep lines around his tired eyes and grey stubble, wearing a cream cable-knit sweater and a silver whistle on a cord around his neck. He bends slightly with both hands positioned just under the bar, spotting. Both faces are clearly visible: we see the young man's face from above and the older man's face upside down in the frame's centre, seen from a low angle at the side of the bench. The room is a small, old basement gym with a worn black rubber floor, a rack of chipped hex dumbbells, a cracked mirror panel, peeling green paint on breeze-block walls and a single barred window high up. The lighting is full-blooded, saturated three-strip Technicolor: hard, sculpted studio key light from the upper left on both faces, with a warm amber gel on one side and a cool teal gel on the other, rich reds, deep greens and glowing, healthy flesh tones, and a subtle painted-backdrop depth to the walls. Graceful, composed, unhurried framing on a 35mm lens at f/4, fine film grain, skin with visible pores and a light sheen of sweat. Nothing has gone wrong yet; the mood is calm, warm and gloriously beautiful. No readable text or logos anywhere. Thanks.

looks.name: The Optimised Image
looks.family: hybrid invented for this film. The name and concept are mine. No existing film does exactly this, as far as I could establish **[unverified]**
looks.pitch: Invented for this film: the picture gets slicker as the app takes over, then a hard flash in the coroner's office. Starts from Martin Parr, through Nosedive, to The Truman Show.
looks.why: the look itself is a character and a threat. Viewers will enjoy Brandon's improvement, and feel uneasy without knowing why. The brighter it gets, the more frightening it gets, so the film runs against the usual dark-means-danger grammar. The last hard flash then hits like a crime-scene photograph.
looks.risk: it is the hardest option to keep consistent, since three looks need three sets of rules and the steps between them must feel gradual. It may read as a clever idea that the audience notices once and then ignores. And Nosedive is close enough that some viewers will just say "Black Mirror".
looks.prompt: A candid colour photograph taken with a cheap compact camera and its built-in flash, close and a little too near, in a cramped budget gym in a small English town. A 22-year-old man named Brandon lies on his back on a worn black vinyl bench press, gripping a loaded steel barbell above his chest, and looks straight up and back toward the man standing over him with a wide, completely trusting, slightly dopey expression. He is skinny and blotchy, with a red cold sore at the corner of his mouth, sweat shining on his forehead, visible pores and uneven pink patches on his cheeks, thin untidy brown hair, a faded cotton t-shirt and baggy grey joggers with a bobbled texture. Gary, a tired man of about fifty, stands at the head of the bench looking down at him, both hands open and tucked just under the bar in a spotter's position. Gary has a broken-veined, ruddy face, heavy eyelids, grey stubble, deep lines at the mouth and a washed-out grey t-shirt that has been washed too many times. Both faces are sharply visible. The flash is harsh and direct, so it flattens the skin to a glossy, saturated pink and throws a hard small shadow behind the barbell onto the bench and wall, while the background falls off darker. Around them: a rubber-matted floor with scuffs, a rack of mismatched iron plates, a cheap mirror with a smeared corner, a flickering strip light overhead, and a pale blue painted breeze-block wall, all in vivid, slightly garish colour. The framing is nearly square, tight and slightly off-level, shot from a low angle near Brandon's head looking up past the bar toward Gary, with a wide-angle compact lens that bends the edges a little and gives fine film-like grain. Nothing has gone wrong yet: the bar is steady and the mood is ordinary and hopeful. Thanks.

subject: Gary spotting Brandon on the bench press, just before anything goes wrong.
